facts_and_myths.claim: Raccoons wash their food in water because their mouths lack salivary glands.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Raccoons have normal salivary glands; wetting their paws stimulates nerve endings and vastly increases tactile sensitivity when examining food.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A raccoon's hands have five nimble digits that can open trash cans, jars, and door handles.

facts_and_myths.claim: Raccoons can remember solutions to complex lock puzzles for over three years.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Laboratory studies have proven raccoons possess extraordinary memory and problem-solving abilities comparable to rhesus monkeys.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Raccoons can rotate their hind feet 180 degrees to descend trees face-first.

name: Honey Badger
visual_anchor: A fearless honey badger with a broad silver-white mantle and sharp claws trotting undeterred across the Kalahari scrub.
core_traits: Renowned worldwide for fearless aggression against lions, hyenas, and venomous snakes
Tough rubbery skin nearly 6 millimeters thick that resists machetes and dog bites
Skin is so loose the animal can twist around inside it to bite back when held
Possesses high resistance to neurotoxic venom from cobras and adders

facts_and_myths.claim: A honey badger can recover and walk away after being bitten by a deadly venomous puff adder.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Honey badgers have evolved mutated muscular nicotinic acetylcholine receptors that provide immunity to cobra and adder venom, allowing them to sleep off bites.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Guinness Book of World Records named the honey badger the world's most fearless creature.

facts_and_myths.claim: Honey badgers primarily consume honey and have a strictly vegetarian diet.
facts_and_myths.explanation: They raid hives mainly for bee brood and larvae rather than honey, and they actively hunt rodents, birds, scorpions, and venomous snakes.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Honey badgers are known tool users, rolling rocks and logs to climb out of walled enclosures.

name: Striped Skunk
visual_anchor: A black-and-white striped skunk raising its bushy plume tail high in warning on a moonlit woodland trail.
core_traits: Famed defense mechanism of spraying an overpowering sulfurous musk up to 3 meters
Striking black coat divided by two bold white stripes forming a 'V' pattern
Stamps front feet and raises tail as a visual warning before spraying
Carnivorous and insectivorous omnivore helpful in controlling garden pests

facts_and_myths.claim: Skunks spray instantaneously without giving any prior warning signals.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Skunks only have enough musk for five to six sprays and take ten days to replenish it; they hiss, stomp front feet, and raise tails first.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Great horned owls have almost no sense of smell and regularly prey on skunks.

facts_and_myths.claim: Skunk spray contains chemical compounds called thiols that can be smelled over a mile away.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Sulfur-based thiols in skunk spray cause intense burning in eyes and nasal passages and can be detected by human noses at parts-per-billion concentrations.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Tomato juice only masks the smell temporarily; hydrogen peroxide and baking soda are needed to neutralize thiols chemically.

name: Wolverine
visual_anchor: A stocky muscular wolverine with dark brown fur and frosty silver face cresting a snowy ridge in the northern taiga.
core_traits: Largest land-dwelling member of the weasel family Mustelidae
Incredible strength allowing it to defend food from wolves and grizzly bears
Hydrophobic dense coat that prevents moisture and frost from sticking
Specialized upper molar rotated 90 degrees to tear through frozen bone and meat

facts_and_myths.claim: Wolverines are fierce enough to kill adult moose trapped in deep winter snow.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Using broad paws that act like snowshoes, wolverines run effortlessly across crusty deep snow and bring down ungulates bogged down in drifts.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A wolverine can travel over 40 kilometers across freezing alpine terrain in a single day.

facts_and_myths.claim: Wolverines are closely related to small wolves and belong to the canine family.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Despite the name 'wolverine', it is a mustelid, closely related to otters, ferrets, and badgers, not canines.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Wolverines emit a pungent musk from anal glands, earning them the nickname 'skunk bear'.

name: Capybara
visual_anchor: A calm, heavy-set capybara basking contentedly at the edge of a South American lagoon with birds resting on its back.
core_traits: Undisputed largest living rodent species on Earth, weighing up to 65 kilograms
Semi-aquatic herbivore native to rivers and wetlands across South America
Partially webbed feet enabling proficient swimming and diving
Famous for an exceptionally calm demeanor and sociability with other animal species

facts_and_myths.claim: Capybaras can remain submerged completely underwater for up to five minutes.
facts_and_myths.explanation: When escaping predators like jaguars or anacondas, capybaras dive and hold their breath underwater, keeping only nostrils above the surface.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Capybara teeth grow continuously throughout life to compensate for grinding tough aquatic grasses.

facts_and_myths.claim: The capybara is a species of wild pig native to the Amazon.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Although historically called 'water pigs', capybaras are true rodents, closely related to guinea pigs and chinchillas.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In the 16th century, the Vatican classified the semi-aquatic capybara as 'fish' so colonists could eat it during Lent.

name: Meerkat
visual_anchor: A slender meerkat sentinel standing upright on its hind legs atop a dusty desert mound, scanning the sky for hawks.
core_traits: Small desert mongoose famed for standing upright on its hind legs as a sentry
Lives in highly cooperative underground colonies called mobs or clans
Dark patches around the eyes act as natural sunglasses against harsh glare
Possesses natural immunity to venomous scorpions and snake stings

facts_and_myths.claim: Meerkats can safely eat venomous scorpions without getting stung.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Adult meerkats teach pups to bite off the venomous stinger first, and they have strong genetic resistance to scorpion venom.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Meerkats take turns acting as sentinels while the rest of the mob forages for insects and tubers.

facts_and_myths.claim: Meerkats are a species of miniature desert primates.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Meerkats belong to the family Herpestidae (mongooses) within the carnivore order Carnivora, entirely distinct from primates.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A meerkat's eyes have a clear protective membrane that shields them while digging through sandy soil.

name: Ring-Tailed Lemur
visual_anchor: A ring-tailed lemur sitting cross-legged with arms outstretched sunbathing on a limestone outcrop in Madagascar.
core_traits: Iconic black-and-white banded tail featuring exactly 13 black rings and 12 white rings
Endemic exclusively to the island of Madagascar
Practices 'stink fights' by rubbing scent gland secretions onto its tail and wafting it at rivals
Social groups are strictly matriarchal, led by dominant females

facts_and_myths.claim: Ring-tailed lemur troops are strictly dominated by alpha females.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Unlike most primates, all adult female ring-tailed lemurs are socially dominant over males and have priority access to food.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In the morning, lemurs sit in a 'yoga' posture facing the sun with bellies exposed to warm up.

facts_and_myths.claim: Ring-tailed lemurs use their long striped tails to hang from tree branches.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Their tails are not prehensile; they cannot grasp branches and are used purely for balance and visual communication.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The word lemur comes from the Latin 'lemures', meaning ghosts or nocturnal spirits.

name: Olive Baboon
visual_anchor: A robust male olive baboon with a heavy gray-green mane and dog-like muzzle striding confidently across the East African savanna.
core_traits: Large Old World monkey recognized by a dog-like elongated muzzle and cheek pouches
Coarse olive-green coat and a prominent broken-arched tail
Highly intelligent and omnivorous primate traveling in large cohesive troops
Males display fearsome dagger-like canine teeth longer than a lion's

facts_and_myths.claim: Male olive baboons possess canine teeth that can be longer than those of adult lions.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A full-grown male baboon's canines can exceed 5 centimeters in length, used primarily for defense and intra-troop displays.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Troops of olive baboons regularly hunt baby gazelles and hares for fresh meat.

facts_and_myths.claim: Baboons are arboreal animals that spend almost their entire lives high in the forest canopy.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Baboons are primarily terrestrial primates that spend most of their days foraging on the ground, climbing trees or cliffs only to sleep safely.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Baboons use over 30 distinct vocalizations, ranging from barks to grunts, to coordinate troop movements.

name: Mandrill
visual_anchor: A massive male mandrill displaying a vivid crimson and cobalt-blue ridged snout and golden beard in a Central African rainforest.
core_traits: World's largest monkey species, exhibiting extreme sexual dimorphism
Spectacular facial coloration featuring bright red bridge and bright blue ribbed flanks
Possesses vivid blue, purple, and scarlet rump coloration that aids group cohesion
Adult males develop enormous yellow beards and massive muscular shoulders

facts_and_myths.claim: The mandrill's bright red and blue skin colors are created by dietary pigments like carotenoids.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The vibrant blue facial colors are generated by light scattering from collagen fibers (structural color), while the red is from blood vessels.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Mandrills can form supergroups (hordes) numbering well over 800 individuals in Gabon.

facts_and_myths.claim: A dominant male mandrill's color brightness increases with higher testosterone and social status.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The intensity of red and blue pigmentation directly correlates with circulating testosterone; deposed males quickly fade.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Mandrill cheek pouches can hold an entire meal's worth of fruit to be eaten later in safety.

name: Bornean Orangutan
visual_anchor: A majestic male Bornean orangutan with wide fleshy cheek pads and long shaggy red-orange hair swinging slowly through the dipterocarp canopy.
core_traits: World's largest tree-dwelling mammal, spending over 90% of its life aloft
Distinctive shaggy reddish-orange coat and extraordinarily long arms spanning over 2 meters
Mature dominant males develop large circular cheek pads called flanges and throat sacs
Extremely intelligent great ape native to the rainforests of Borneo

facts_and_myths.claim: Orangutans share roughly 97% of their DNA with human beings.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Genetic sequencing shows that orangutans share around 96.9% of identical genetic material with humans, making them one of our closest living relatives.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Orangutans build fresh, elaborate sleeping nests out of bent branches and leaves every single evening.

facts_and_myths.claim: Orangutans live in large, noisy social troops similar to chimpanzees.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Orangutans are the most solitary of all great apes; adults rarely socialize outside of mating, due to the dispersed nature of canopy fruit.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: An orangutan's arm span can reach 2.2 meters, significantly longer than its standing height.

name: Dromedary Camel
visual_anchor: A sturdy single-humped dromedary camel with long curved eyelashes standing tall amidst windswept Saharan dunes.
core_traits: Renowned 'Ship of the Desert' equipped with a single prominent fatty hump on its back
Features double rows of long eyelashes and sealable nostrils to block sandstorms
Specialized oval red blood cells that continue flowing even during extreme dehydration
Capable of drinking up to 100 liters of water in just ten minutes

facts_and_myths.claim: A camel's hump is a storage tank filled with water.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Camel humps store energy-rich adipose fat, not water; concentrating fat in one spot allows the rest of the body to cool efficiently.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: When starved of food, a camel's hump shrinks and droops over to one side.

facts_and_myths.claim: Camels can withstand losing up to 30% of their body weight in water without dying.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Most mammals succumb to heart failure at 12-14% water loss, but camels endure 30% loss thanks to unique oval red blood cells.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Camels have broad padded feet that spread out to prevent sinking into soft sand.

name: Llama
visual_anchor: A tall woolly llama with banana-shaped upright ears standing proudly against a scenic backdrop of Andean peaks in Peru.
core_traits: South American camelid domesticated thousands of years ago as a beast of burden
Distinguished by long, curved 'banana-shaped' ears and a high head posture
Infamous for spitting regurgitated stomach contents when irritated or challenged
Highly valued for carrying loads over steep high-altitude mountain trails

facts_and_myths.claim: Llamas spit only when provoked by humans.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Llamas primarily spit at each other to establish dominance, discipline troop members, or reject unwanted suitors; spitting at humans is rare unless mistreated.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Llamas are widely employed as livestock guard animals to protect sheep flocks from coyotes.

facts_and_myths.claim: A llama will stubbornly lie down on the ground and refuse to move if overloaded.
facts_and_myths.explanation: If a pack exceeds 25-30% of its body weight, a llama will sit down, hiss, spit, and refuse to budge until the weight is lightened.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Llama blood contains unusually high concentrations of hemoglobin to thrive in oxygen-thin Andean air.

name: Alpaca
visual_anchor: A gentle, fluffy alpaca with dense fleece and short spear-shaped ears grazing in a high Andean valley.
core_traits: Domesticated Andean camelid bred specifically for luxurious, super-soft fleece
Noticeably smaller than the llama, with straight, spear-shaped ears and a blunt face
Produces hypoallergenic wool that contains no lanolin and is warmer than sheep's wool
Docile herd animal that communicates through soft hums and clucks

facts_and_myths.claim: Alpaca fleece is naturally water-resistant and fire-retardant.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Alpaca fiber contains microscopic air pockets that make it lightweight, thermal, water-repellent, and naturally resistant to flame.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Alpacas use a communal dung pile, which helps prevent the spread of parasites in pastures.

facts_and_myths.claim: Alpacas and llamas are just two different names for the exact same animal.
facts_and_myths.explanation: They are distinct species; alpacas were domesticated from the wild vicuna for fleece, while llamas were domesticated from the guanaco as pack animals.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Alpacas hum when they are curious, content, worried, or bored.

name: American Bison
visual_anchor: A massive American bison bull with a shaggy dark brown shoulder hump and curved horns kicking up dust on the Great Plains.
core_traits: Heaviest native terrestrial animal in North America, weighing up to 1,000 kilograms
Massive shoulder hump composed of powerful muscles that support snow-plowing head movements
Dense shaggy winter coat and short, sharp curved horns on both males and females
Capable of sprinting at speeds exceeding 55 km/h despite immense size

facts_and_myths.claim: American bison can jump over fences that are nearly six feet tall.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Despite their colossal weight, bison are remarkably agile jumpers capable of clearing vertical fences up to 1.8 meters high.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Bison use their massive heads like snowplows to sweep aside deep drifts and reach grass in winter.

facts_and_myths.claim: The American bison is biologically a true buffalo.
facts_and_myths.explanation: True buffaloes are native to Africa and Asia (like the Cape buffalo and water buffalo); the American bison belongs to the distinct genus Bison.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In the 1800s, bison numbers collapsed from over 30 million to fewer than 1,000 before successful conservation efforts.

name: African Buffalo
visual_anchor: A formidable Cape buffalo bull with fused boss horns glaring sternly across an African waterhole.
core_traits: Member of the legendary African 'Big Five' game animals
Adult males possess a continuous bone shield over the forehead known as a 'boss'
Renowned for fierce collective defense against lion prides
Never successfully domesticated due to an unpredictable, aggressive temperament

facts_and_myths.claim: Cape buffaloes actively mob and kill lion cubs to protect their herd.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Buffaloes demonstrate proactive defense; herds will deliberately seek out and trample lion prides and kill young cubs to reduce future predator threats.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Cape buffalo's fused horn base is so dense that it can deflect high-caliber hunting rifle bullets.

facts_and_myths.claim: African buffaloes are easily herded and domesticated by local pastoralists.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Unlike Asian water buffaloes, African buffaloes have an extremely aggressive, erratic temperament and have resisted all domestication attempts.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Hunters dubbed the Cape buffalo 'The Black Death' and 'Widowmaker' due to its habit of ambushing pursuers.

name: Wild Yak
visual_anchor: A colossal wild yak bull with sweeping horns and an ankle-length shaggy skirt standing amidst freezing Tibetan plateau snow.
core_traits: Colossal high-altitude bovine native to the remote Himalayas and Tibetan Plateau
Dense fleece covered by an outer skirt of long shaggy hair that reaches the ground
Massive lungs and heart adapted to low-oxygen environments above 4,000 meters
Sweeps curved horns spanning nearly a meter to shovel through frozen snow

facts_and_myths.claim: Wild yaks secrete a red substance in their sweat that acts as a natural waterproofing agent.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Their sweat contains a sticky, reddish resin-like substance that matts their dense fleece together, providing complete waterproofing against blizzards.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Yaks do not produce a normal moo; instead, they make low guttural grunts, earning the domestic yak the name Bos grunniens (grunting ox).

facts_and_myths.claim: Yaks easily overheat and suffer if transported to low, warm altitudes.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Adapted strictly for sub-zero alpine climates, yaks lack functional sweat glands on most of their body and suffer heat exhaustion above 15 degrees Celsius.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Yak milk is rich and pink-tinged immediately after calving, yielding nutritious butter and cheese.

name: Blackbuck Antelope
visual_anchor: A striking male blackbuck with long ringed spiral horns and contrasting black-and-white coat bounding across an Indian grassland.
core_traits: Slender antelope famed for spectacular spiral corkscrew horns
Adult males display a dramatic two-tone black upper body and pure white underbelly
One of the fastest land animals in Asia, reaching speeds up to 80 km/h
Performs high bouncing jumps into the air known as stotting or pronking

facts_and_myths.claim: Female blackbucks grow the same long corkscrew horns as males.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Blackbucks display strong sexual dimorphism; females are light fawn-colored and almost always hornless, while males develop long spiraled horns.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A blackbuck's spiral horns can have three to five turns and reach up to 70 centimeters in length.

facts_and_myths.claim: Blackbucks can sustain top running speeds over long distances to outlast pursuit.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Unlike cheetahs that tire after a brief sprint, blackbucks can maintain high speeds of 60 to 70 km/h for several kilometers.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Historically, Indian royalty trained cheetahs specifically to hunt swift blackbucks.

name: Thomson's Gazelle
visual_anchor: A fleet-footed Thomson's gazelle with a black flank stripe stotting high into the air on the Serengeti plains.
core_traits: One of the best-known gazelles in East Africa, universally recognized by a dark flank stripe
Light brown coat, white rump, and curved ringed horns present on both sexes
Performs high vertical leaps called stotting to signal alertness to predators
Top sprinting speed reaches nearly 80 km/h, making it a primary prey of cheetahs

facts_and_myths.claim: Gazelles leap stiff-legged into the air (stotting) to taunt stalking predators.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Stotting is an honest signal that communicates to cheetahs that the gazelle is fit, healthy, and alert, often causing predators to abandon the chase.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A Thomson's gazelle constantly wags its short black tail back and forth like a metronome while grazing.

facts_and_myths.claim: Thomson's gazelles can easily be caught by lions in a direct footrace.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Lions top out at roughly 60 km/h, while gazelles reach 80 km/h and can make sharp 90-degree turns that heavy big cats cannot match.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: They obtain most of their daily water requirements directly from dew and moisture in grass.

name: Impala
visual_anchor: A graceful male impala with sweeping lyre-shaped horns bounding effortlessly over a tall bush in the African woodland.
core_traits: Medium-sized African antelope renowned for spectacular jumping ability
Can leap up to 3 meters into the air and cover distances of over 10 meters in a single bound
Adult males possess long, ridged, lyre-shaped horns
Glossy reddish-tan coat with distinct black vertical stripes on the tail and thighs

facts_and_myths.claim: Female impalas grow smaller curved horns used for herd defense.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Female impalas are completely hornless; only males develop the sweeping lyre-shaped horns used in territorial clashes.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Impalas have specialized grooming teeth with movable incisors used to comb ticks from each other's fur.

facts_and_myths.claim: Impalas have scent glands hidden in black tufts on their rear heels.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Black tufts on the lower hind legs enclose metatarsal scent glands that leave chemical scent trails when leaping away from danger.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: When startled, an entire herd will explode into chaotic zig-zag leaping to confuse predators.

name: Blue Wildebeest
visual_anchor: A dense column of blue wildebeest charging across the crocodile-filled Mara River during the Great Migration.
core_traits: Renowned participant in the famous annual East African Great Migration of over 1.5 million animals
Robust cow-like body with a heavy head, black beard, and slate-gray striped flanks
Curved horns on both sexes resembling those of cattle
Calves can stand and run within seven minutes of being born

facts_and_myths.claim: Wildebeest calves are helpless and must be hidden in dens for weeks after birth.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Wildebeest calves are precocial; they stand within minutes and can keep pace with the galloping herd within an hour of birth.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Over 500,000 wildebeest calves are born during a synchronized two-to-three-week window each February.

facts_and_myths.claim: Wildebeest rely on an innate sense of smell and sound to detect rainstorms dozens of miles away.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Wildebeest track fresh pasture by following the scent of petrichor (rain on dry earth) and the rumble of distant thunder.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The name 'gnu' comes from the Khoikhoi language imitating the animal's loud, abrupt snort.

name: Common Warthog
visual_anchor: A sturdy warthog trotting upright across the savannah with its antenna-like tail held straight up in the air.
core_traits: African wild pig distinguished by four facial wart-like bumps and curling ivory tusks
Trots with its slender tail held vertically erect like an antenna
Kneels on padded wrists to graze on short grasses and dig for roots
Backs into underground burrows rear-first so its sharp tusks face the entrance

facts_and_myths.claim: Warthog facial 'warts' are actual cancerous growths or tumors.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The 'warts' are protective pads of thickened cartilage and skin that shield the eyes and face during fights with rival males.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Warthogs regularly allow mongooses to climb all over them to groom and eat ticks off their skin.

facts_and_myths.claim: Warthogs always enter burrows backwards to defend themselves against predators.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Backing in rear-first leaves their formidable tusks pointed outward, ready to impale any leopard or hyena that attempts to enter.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A warthog's upper tusks can curl up to 25 centimeters in length.

name: Wild Boar
visual_anchor: A formidable dark-bristled wild boar rooting through autumnal oak leaf litter with razor-sharp tusks gleaming.
core_traits: Wild ancestor of the domestic pig, native across Eurasia and North Africa
Coarse bristly dark coat, prominent shoulder ridge, and straight tail
Equipped with self-sharpening lower tusks that continuously rub against upper teeth
Highly intelligent and adaptable omnivore capable of defending against wolves

facts_and_myths.claim: A wild boar's tusks constantly sharpen themselves as the animal chews.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The lower canines grow continuously and hone against the shorter upper tusks, maintaining a razor-sharp cutting edge.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In medieval Europe, hunting a wild boar on foot with a spear was considered the ultimate test of courage.

facts_and_myths.claim: Wild boars have poor senses of smell and rely purely on exceptional eyesight.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Boars have notoriously poor eyesight, but their sense of smell is so acute they can locate acorns and truffles buried deep underground.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Striped boar piglets are called 'humbugs' due to their distinctive cream-and-brown longitudinal camouflage stripes.

name: European Hedgehog
visual_anchor: A small nocturnal European hedgehog rolled into a tight spiny ball amidst fallen autumn leaves in a garden.
core_traits: Small nocturnal mammal covered in approximately 5,000 to 7,000 sharp keratin spines
Defensive reflex of rolling into an impenetrable tight prickly sphere
Practices 'self-anointing', frothing saliva on its quills when encountering new scents
Beneficial garden insectivore feeding on slugs, beetles, and worms

facts_and_myths.claim: Hedgehogs can shoot their sharp quills outward like arrows when threatened.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Hedgehog spines are firmly rooted modified hairs; they cannot be launched or detached voluntarily.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Hedgehogs are naturally immune to certain snake venoms and can safely eat small adders.

facts_and_myths.claim: Hedgehogs lick pungent foreign substances and smear frothy saliva onto their spines.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Known as self-anointing, the exact reason is debated, but it is believed to provide scent camouflage or defensive toxicity.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Baby hedgehogs (hoglets) are born with soft spines covered by fluid-filled skin to protect the mother during birth.

name: North American Porcupine
visual_anchor: A large stout porcupine perched high in a snowy hemlock tree, bristling with thousands of barbed quills.
core_traits: Second-largest rodent in North America, covered in over 30,000 barbed quills
Quills feature microscopic backward-facing barbs that pull deeper into predator flesh
Excellent tree climber with long curved claws and pebble-textured soles
Herbivore with a notorious craving for natural salts and mineral-rich bark

facts_and_myths.claim: Porcupines can throw or shoot their quills at attacking predators from several feet away.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Quills cannot be thrown or launched; they detach easily on direct contact when the porcupine thrashes its tail against an attacker.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The fisher, a forest mustelid, is one of the few predators specialized in flipping porcupines over to attack the unquilled belly.

facts_and_myths.claim: Porcupine quills have microscopic barbs that cause them to work deeper into tissue with muscle movement.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Each quill has thousands of backward-pointing shingle-like scales that make removal painful and drive the quill inward.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Porcupines love salt so much they often chew on canoe paddles, axe handles, and vehicle tires to lick road salt.

name: Nine-Banded Armadillo
visual_anchor: An armored nine-banded armadillo foraging with its snout buried in soft forest dirt under warm morning sunshine.
core_traits: Distinctive bony carapace composed of nine movable dermal armor bands
Prolific burrower that digs extensive underground dens to escape heat and predators
Almost always gives birth to genetically identical quadruplets
Startle reflex involves jumping three to four feet straight up into the air

facts_and_myths.claim: Nine-banded armadillos roll themselves into a complete, impenetrable armored ball when attacked.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Only the three-banded armadillo can roll into a sphere; nine-banded armadillos flee into burrows or jump vertically to startle predators.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Armadillos can hold their breath for up to six minutes and inflate their stomach with air to swim across rivers.

facts_and_myths.claim: Female nine-banded armadillos consistently give birth to identical quadruplets derived from a single egg.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Through obligate polyembryony, every litter produces four genetically identical offspring of the same sex.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Armadillos are one of the few non-human animals known to naturally contract leprosy, aiding medical research.

name: Giant Anteater
visual_anchor: A large giant anteater with a bushy banner tail and long tubular snout ripping open a termite mound on the Brazilian pantanal.
core_traits: Largest of all anteaters, completely toothless with a tubular elongated snout
Sticky tongue measuring up to 60 centimeters that can flick in and out 150 times a minute
Enormous hooked front claws capable of tearing into concrete-hard termite mounds
Flies a massive bushy tail used like a blanket when sleeping

facts_and_myths.claim: Giant anteaters have sharp teeth in the back of their jaws to chew insects.
facts_and_myths.explanation: They belong to the suborder Vermilingua and are completely toothless; strong stomach muscles and swallowed sand grind insects.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A giant anteater can consume over 30,000 ants and termites in a single day.

facts_and_myths.claim: A cornered giant anteater can use its front claws to fatally wound a jaguar.
facts_and_myths.explanation: When threatened, the anteater rears up on its hind legs and delivers crushing hugs with four-inch claws designed to crack cement-like mounds.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: They spend no more than a minute feeding at any single termite nest to avoid destroying the colony.

name: Fruit Bat
visual_anchor: A giant golden-crowned flying fox hanging upside-down by its clawed feet wrapped in dark leathery wings in a tropical fruit tree.
core_traits: Among the largest bats on Earth, with wingspans reaching up to 1.5 to 1.7 meters
Fox-like canine face with large eyes and prominent ears, lacking a tail
Relies on keen eyesight and acute sense of smell rather than echolocation
Crucial keystone pollinator and seed disperser across tropical rainforests

facts_and_myths.claim: Fruit bats navigate pitch-black caves primarily using sophisticated sonar echolocation.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Unlike microbats, most megabats (flying foxes) have completely lost echolocation; they navigate using excellent nocturnal vision and acute smell.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Fruit bats crush fruit in their mouths to swallow only the juice, spitting out the pulp and seeds.

facts_and_myths.claim: Fruit bats are vital for the survival of tropical plants including durian and wild bananas.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Many commercial and wild tropical trees rely exclusively on large fruit bats for nocturnal pollination and long-distance seed dispersal.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The giant golden-crowned flying fox can have a wingspan of 1.7 meters while weighing only about 1.2 kilograms.

name: Common Vampire Bat
visual_anchor: A small agile vampire bat creeping silently on all fours across a wooden beam in a dark South American roosting cave.
core_traits: Only known parasitic mammal that feeds exclusively on the blood of other animals (hematophagy)
Specialized infrared heat-sensing pit on the nose to locate warm blood vessels under skin
Razor-sharp grooved incisors that shave hair and slice painless tiny wounds
Remarkably agile on the ground, capable of bounding, running, and jumping

facts_and_myths.claim: Vampire bats suck blood through hollow fangs like drinking straws.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Vampire bats make a tiny painless puncture with their incisors and lap up the flowing blood with their grooved tongues.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Their saliva contains an anticoagulant enzyme named 'Draculin' that prevents blood from clotting while feeding.

facts_and_myths.claim: Vampire bats will regurgitate stored blood to feed starving roost-mates in their colony.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because a vampire bat will starve if it misses a meal for 48 hours, they engage in reciprocal food sharing, donating blood to hungry peers.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Vampire bats are the only bats that can walk, run, and gallop on the ground using their folded wing wrists.

name: Northern Flying Squirrel
visual_anchor: A furry northern flying squirrel with huge nocturnal black eyes gliding between pine trunks with its furry patagium membrane fully spread.
core_traits: Nocturnal rodent possessing a furred gliding membrane called a patagium stretching from wrist to ankle
Enormous dark eyes adapted for night navigation through dense boreal forests
Uses a broad, flat furry tail like an aerodynamic rudder to steer and brake mid-flight
Capable of gliding distances exceeding 65 meters across forest canopies

facts_and_myths.claim: Flying squirrels fly by actively flapping their skin membranes like bat wings.
facts_and_myths.explanation: They cannot achieve powered flight; they leap from elevated branches and glide downward using aerodynamics, steering with their flat tail.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Under ultraviolet blacklight, flying squirrel fur glows a striking vivid hot pink.

facts_and_myths.claim: A flying squirrel can execute 180-degree mid-air turns while gliding.
facts_and_myths.explanation: By adjusting the tension of their patagium membranes with a specialized wrist cartilage rod, they perform sharp evasive aerial maneuvers.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Flying squirrels consume mostly subterranean truffles and lichens, spreading beneficial mycorrhizal fungi across forest soils.

name: Walrus
visual_anchor: A massive wrinkled bull walrus with two-foot ivory tusks and dense whiskers hauled out on an Arctic ice floe.
core_traits: Massive Arctic pinniped distinguished by elongated ivory tusks in both sexes
Prominent bristly moustache of sensitive whiskers called vibrissae
Thick blubber layer up to 10 centimeters deep that turns pink when basking in the sun
Forages on ocean floor clams using powerful hydraulic water jet suction

facts_and_myths.claim: Walruses use their giant tusks like pickaxes to haul their heavy bodies onto sea ice.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Their genus name Odobenus literally means 'tooth-walker', referring to their ability to anchor tusks into ice while dragging themselves out.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A walrus can suction the meat out of a clam shell in less than a second without swallowing the shell.

facts_and_myths.claim: Walruses hunt polar bears and seals as their primary dietary prey.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Walruses are benthic foragers that consume clams, crabs, and marine worms off the shallow ocean floor, rarely eating seal meat.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Blood vessels in walrus blubber constrict in freezing water making them pale gray, but dilate in sun turning them rosy pink.

name: California Sea Lion
visual_anchor: A sleek chocolate-brown California sea lion barking boisterously while balancing effortlessly on a coastal harbor pier.
core_traits: Agile 'eared seal' characterized by external ear flaps and powerful foreflippers
Capable of rotating hind flippers forward to walk, run, and climb on all fours on land
Famous for loud, incessant barking vocalizations and playful intelligence
Adult males develop a prominent bony crest on the top of the skull called a sagittal crest

facts_and_myths.claim: Sea lions are true seals that cannot walk on land using their hind flippers.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Sea lions are otariids (eared seals) that can rotate their pelvis and hind flippers forward to gallop on land, unlike true earless seals.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The U.S. Navy trains California sea lions to locate lost underwater equipment and detect naval mines.

facts_and_myths.claim: California sea lions can swim at bursts exceeding 30 km/h and dive over 250 meters deep.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Using large wing-like pectoral flippers for underwater propulsion, they are extraordinarily fast and agile marine hunters.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Sea lions can hold their breath for 10 to 15 minutes by drastically slowing their heart rate.

name: Harbor Seal
visual_anchor: A spotted silvery-gray harbor seal resting on coastal kelp rocks with its head and tail tilted upward in a banana pose.
core_traits: Widespread true seal (phocid) lacking external ear flaps and possessing short front flippers
Moves on land by undulating its belly in a caterpillar-like motion called 'galumphing'
Mottled spotted coat ranging from silver-gray to dark charcoal
Frequently rests in the characteristic curved 'banana pose' to keep extremities warm

facts_and_myths.claim: Harbor seals can use their sensitive whiskers to track the hydrodynamic wake of a swimming fish.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Their beaded whiskers (vibrissae) can detect the water trail left by a swimming fish up to 100 meters away, even in total darkness.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Harbor seal pups can swim within minutes of birth and often ride on their mother's back in strong currents.

facts_and_myths.claim: Harbor seals have external ear flaps just like sea lions.
facts_and_myths.explanation: As true seals, they have no external ear flaps, only tiny pinhole ear openings on the sides of their head.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Harbor seals regularly sleep completely underwater, surfacing periodically to breathe without waking up.

name: Southern Elephant Seal
visual_anchor: A gigantic male elephant seal with a bulbous proboscis roaring defiantly on a stormy sub-Antarctic beach.
core_traits: Colossal marine carnivore, undisputed largest pinniped and largest member of Carnivora on Earth
Adult bulls weigh up to 4,000 kilograms and grow a bulbous inflatable snout (proboscis)
Deepest diving air-breathing carnivore, recorded diving deeper than 2,000 meters
Bulls engage in violent beach battles for control of breeding harems

facts_and_myths.claim: Southern elephant seals can dive continuously for two hours without returning to the surface.
facts_and_myths.explanation: They have massive blood volumes loaded with hemoglobin and myoglobin, allowing recorded dives of over 120 minutes down to 2,388 meters.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Male elephant seals can weigh up to eight times more than adult females, showing the highest sexual dimorphism among mammals.

facts_and_myths.claim: An elephant seal's trunk-like proboscis is used for breathing underwater like a snorkel.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The proboscis acts as an acoustic resonance chamber to amplify loud, roaring challenges against rival bulls on land.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: They spend over 80% of their life at sea and spend only two minutes at the surface between deep foraging dives.

name: Beluga Whale
visual_anchor: A pure white beluga whale gliding gracefully under Arctic sea ice with a rounded, flexible bulbous forehead.
core_traits: Arctic cetacean universally recognizable by its pure white adult skin and smiling mouth
Possesses a flexible melon on its forehead capable of changing shape for echolocation
Lacks a dorsal fin to maneuver easily beneath thick sheets of pack ice
Nicknamed the 'Sea Canary' due to high-pitched chirps, whistles, and squeaks

facts_and_myths.claim: Beluga whales are born pure white and retain the same color their entire lives.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Beluga calves are born dark gray or brown and gradually lighten over several years, reaching pure white adulthood around age 8 to 14.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Unlike most whales, a beluga's neck vertebrae are unfused, allowing it to turn its head up, down, and side-to-side.

facts_and_myths.claim: Beluga whales can swim backwards to navigate through tight crevices in pack ice.
facts_and_myths.explanation: With flexible broad pectoral flippers and high maneuverability, belugas are one of the few whales capable of backward swimming.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Belugas can change the shape of their forehead melon by blowing air around their nasal sinuses.

name: Narwhal
visual_anchor: A mottled gray narwhal surfacing in a crack of Arctic sea ice, its long spiraled ivory tusk gleaming in the cold sun.
core_traits: Famed 'Unicorn of the Sea' possessing a long, spiraled ivory tusk protruding from its upper lip
The tusk is an elongated canine tooth containing millions of sensory nerve endings
Endemic year-round resident of the freezing Arctic waters around Greenland, Canada, and Russia
Lacks a dorsal fin to freely swim and surface amidst jagged pack ice

facts_and_myths.claim: The narwhal's long spiral horn is actually an overgrown canine tooth.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The tusk is a modified left upper canine tooth that spirals counter-clockwise and can grow up to 3 meters in length.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The tusk is porous and packed with 10 million nerve endings, functioning as a sensory organ for salinity and temperature.

facts_and_myths.claim: Narwhals use their long tusks to spear large fish like cod before eating them.
facts_and_myths.explanation: They do not impale prey; they use suction to swallow fish whole, though they occasionally use the tusk to stun Arctic cod with quick taps.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In medieval Europe, traded narwhal tusks were sold as authentic unicorn horns worth many times their weight in gold.

name: Bowhead Whale
visual_anchor: A massive dark-bodied bowhead whale with a white chin breaching through an open lead in thick Arctic pack ice.
core_traits: Longest-lived mammal on Earth, capable of exceeding 200 years of age
Possesses the thickest blubber layer of any animal, reaching up to 50 centimeters thick
Massive triangular skull capable of shattering sea ice up to 60 centimeters thick
Bears the longest baleen plates of any whale, hanging up to 4 meters long

facts_and_myths.claim: Bowhead whales can live for more than two centuries in Arctic waters.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Scientists discovered ancient stone harpoon points embedded in living bowheads and eye lens amino acid dating confirmed lifespans past 200 years.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Bowhead whales possess unique genetic mutations that protect them against cancer and cellular aging.

facts_and_myths.claim: Bowhead whales migrate to tropical waters every winter to give birth in warm lagoons.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Unlike gray or humpback whales, bowheads are permanent residents of Arctic waters and never leave the cold polar oceans.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Their mouth accounts for nearly one-third of their entire body length.

name: Sperm Whale
visual_anchor: A colossal dark gray sperm whale diving vertically into the abyss, its massive triangular tail flukes lifting against the open ocean.
core_traits: Largest toothed predator on Earth, reaching lengths up to 18 to 20 meters
Possesses the largest brain of any known animal in history, weighing nearly 9 kilograms
Giant squared head containing the spermaceti organ, producing the loudest sounds in the animal kingdom
Specialized deep-sea hunter that dives kilometers down to battle giant squids

facts_and_myths.claim: Sperm whale echolocation clicks can generate acoustic pulses exceeding 230 decibels.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Sperm whales emit the loudest biological sound on Earth, powerful enough to vibrate through human bodies and stun prey underwater.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Ambergris, a rare waxy substance used in luxury perfumes, is formed in the digestive tract of sperm whales around squid beaks.

facts_and_myths.claim: Sperm whales chew giant squids into small pieces using teeth in both the upper and lower jaws.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Sperm whales have functional teeth only in their narrow lower jaw; the upper jaw has sockets, and they swallow giant squid whole through suction.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Sperm whales sleep vertically, suspended upright in open water like giant floating logs.

name: Leopard Seal
visual_anchor: A serpentine leopard seal with spotted silver-gray skin and a reptilian skull patrolling beneath an Antarctic ice shelf.
core_traits: Formidable apex predator of the Southern Ocean, second only to orcas in Antarctic waters
Slender, reptilian-like head with powerful jaws opening nearly 180 degrees
Massive canine teeth for tearing penguin flesh alongside unique cusped molars to filter krill
Named for black leopard-like spotting across its neck, shoulders, and belly

facts_and_myths.claim: Leopard seals feed exclusively on penguins and warm-blooded seals.
facts_and_myths.explanation: While famous for hunting penguins and seal pups, krill actually makes up about 45% of their diet, filtered using specialized interlocking molars.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Leopard seal females are larger than males, growing up to 3.5 meters long and weighing over 500 kilograms.

facts_and_myths.claim: Leopard seals 'skin' penguins before eating them by vigorously thrashing them against the ocean surface.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because they lack chewing teeth, leopard seals whip penguins back and forth across the water until the carcass is stripped of feathers and skin.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Leopard seals produce rhythmic, underwater singing vocalizations during the austral summer mating season.

name: Coyote
visual_anchor: A cunning tawny-gray coyote howling at twilight on a desert ridge with saguaro cacti silhouetted against the sky.
core_traits: Highly intelligent and adaptable canine native throughout North and Central America
Tawny-gray fur, pointed bushy tail held downward while running, and slender yellow eyes
Famous for a wide repertoire of high-pitched yips, barks, and howls at night
Has expanded its range into suburban neighborhoods and cities despite intensive human pressure

facts_and_myths.claim: Coyotes always run with their bushy tails held straight out horizontally behind them like wolves.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Coyotes typically run with their tails held downward at a low angle, which is a key visual trait distinguishing them from wolves in motion.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Coyotes and American badgers often form cooperative hunting partnerships to catch burrowing prairie dogs.

facts_and_myths.claim: Coyotes can run at top speeds of over 60 km/h and leap over eight-foot fences.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Their incredible speed and agility allow them to run down jackrabbits and easily clear residential property fences.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The name coyote comes from the Aztec Nahuatl word coyotl, meaning 'trickster'.

name: Dingo
visual_anchor: A lean ginger-gold dingo with white-sock paws standing alert against the red earth of the Australian Outback.
core_traits: Apex land predator of the Australian continent, descended from ancient semi-domesticated dogs
Ginger or sandy-golden coat with white markings on the chest, muzzle, and paws
Cannot bark like domestic dogs; communicates through eerie, wolf-like choruses of howls
Features highly flexible wrist and ankle joints that allow it to climb rocky escarpments

facts_and_myths.claim: Pure dingoes bark continuously to defend territory just like domestic dogs.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Pure dingoes do not bark repeatedly; they produce single sharp alarm coughs and communicate primarily through sustained vocal howls.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Dingo Fence in south-eastern Australia spans 5,614 kilometers, one of the longest man-made structures on Earth.

facts_and_myths.claim: Dingoes have highly flexible wrists that allow them to turn door handles and climb trees.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Their flexible joints enable dingoes to rotate paws like hands, climb rocks, and squeeze through small gaps inaccessible to domestic dogs.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Dingoes breed only once per year, whereas domestic dogs typically breed twice annually.

name: Fennec Fox
visual_anchor: A tiny cream-colored fennec fox with enormous upright bat-like ears sitting in the warm sand of the Sahara Desert.
core_traits: Smallest species of the canine family (Canidae) in the world, weighing barely 1.5 kilograms
Huge ears measuring up to 15 centimeters long that radiate body heat and detect subterranean insects
Cream-colored sandy coat reflecting desert sunlight and providing natural camouflage
Heavily furred paw pads that protect against scorching desert sand

facts_and_myths.claim: A fennec fox's massive ears are used solely for hearing distant sounds.
facts_and_myths.explanation: While they provide exceptional acoustic sensitivity to hear insects digging underground, their primary evolutionary role is heat dissipation via dense blood vessels.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Fennec foxes can jump 60 centimeters vertically and over one meter forward from a standstill.

facts_and_myths.claim: Fennec foxes can survive indefinitely without drinking liquid water.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Their kidneys are adapted to minimize water loss, and they extract 100% of their hydration from the moisture in insects, rodents, and berries.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Dense fur on the soles of their feet acts like snowshoes, insulating against searing hot sand.

name: Arctic Fox
visual_anchor: A pristine white arctic fox diving headfirst into deep snow to capture lemmings under a pale polar sky.
core_traits: Cold-adapted northern canine that shifts coat color from brilliant white in winter to brown in summer
Possesses the warmest insulating fur of any mammal, surviving temperatures down to minus 50 Celsius
Short rounded ears, compact muzzle, and short legs to minimize surface area heat loss
Famed for performing dramatic high-leaping headfirst dives into snowdrifts to catch lemmings

facts_and_myths.claim: Arctic foxes retain their pure snow-white fur all year round.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In summer, their coat sheds and changes to a mottled brown and gray to blend in with tundra rocks and vegetation.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: An Arctic fox's metabolism does not even start shivering until temperatures drop below minus 70 degrees Celsius.

facts_and_myths.claim: Arctic foxes frequently follow polar bears across sea ice to scavenge leftover seal scraps.
facts_and_myths.explanation: They trail behind apex polar bears for miles across the pack ice, feeding opportunistically on fatty seal blubber remnants.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Their foot pads are covered in dense fur, earning them the species name lagopus ('hare-footed').

name: Tasmanian Devil
visual_anchor: A stocky black Tasmanian devil with a white chest crescent baring its pink mouth in a loud guttural screech.
core_traits: World's largest surviving carnivorous marsupial, endemic exclusively to the island of Tasmania
Possesses the strongest bite force relative to body mass of any living mammalian land carnivore
Emits blood-curdling screeches and coughs that earned it the name 'devil' from early settlers
Devours entire carcasses including bones, teeth, and fur with heavy crush-resistant jaws

facts_and_myths.claim: Tasmanian devils store excess energy and body fat in their tails.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A thick, plump tail indicates a well-nourished, healthy devil, while a thin tail is a sign of starvation or disease.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A Tasmanian devil can consume up to 40% of its body weight in meat in just thirty minutes.

facts_and_myths.claim: Tasmanian devils are aggressive pack hunters that chase down sheep and kangaroos across open fields.
facts_and_myths.explanation: They are predominantly solitary nocturnal scavengers that feed on carrion and slow prey rather than running down healthy large livestock.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: When stressed, a Tasmanian devil's ears turn bright red due to increased blood flow.

name: Shortfin Mako Shark
visual_anchor: A metallic-blue shortfin mako shark rocketing through deep indigo pelagic waters with crescent tail beating at high speed.
core_traits: Undisputed fastest swimming shark in the world, capable of burst speeds over 70 km/h
Sleek hydrodynamic body with brilliant metallic indigo-blue dorsal coloring and snowy white belly
Endothermic circulatory system that keeps its muscles and brain warmer than surrounding water
Famed for spectacular aerial leaps reaching up to 9 meters out of the water

facts_and_myths.claim: Shortfin mako sharks can leap higher into the air than any other shark species.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Propelled by an immense crescent tail and streamlined form, makos can launch themselves up to 9 meters (30 feet) clear out of the sea.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Mako sharks have tiny tooth-like dermal denticles that flex like fish scales, reducing hydrodynamic drag by 40%.

facts_and_myths.claim: Mako sharks are cold-blooded animals whose muscles remain the exact temperature of the water.
facts_and_myths.explanation: They possess a specialized vascular counter-current heat exchanger (rete mirabile) that keeps core swimming muscles up to 7 degrees Celsius warmer than the sea.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A shortfin mako shark can travel more than 2,000 kilometers in just over a month.

name: Tiger Shark
visual_anchor: A massive tiger shark with dark vertical flank stripes cruising effortlessly across a shallow tropical coral lagoon.
core_traits: Large apex predator recognized by dark vertical tiger-like stripes that fade with age
Uniquely shaped cockscomb teeth with curved serrations designed to crack sea turtle carapaces
Notorious 'wastebasket of the sea' known for consuming license plates, tires, and metal debris
Second only to the great white shark in recorded encounters with humans

facts_and_myths.claim: Tiger sharks possess specialized teeth specifically evolved to cut through hard turtle shells.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Their teeth have heavily calcified sideways-curving cusps with secondary serrations that slice cleanly through bony turtle carapaces like a circular saw.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Marine biologists have found intact suits of armor, horse skulls, and unopened tin cans inside tiger shark stomachs.

facts_and_myths.claim: The vertical tiger stripes on a tiger shark become darker and bolder as the shark grows older.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The stripes are most prominent and vivid on juveniles and fade gradually as the shark reaches mature adulthood, becoming nearly solid gray.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Tiger sharks have an acute sense of smell and electroreceptive ampullae that can detect heartbeats of buried stingrays.

name: Bull Shark
visual_anchor: A stout, blunt-snouted bull shark cruising turbid brown water near a tropical river delta.
core_traits: Stout, heavy-bodied predatory shark named for its broad blunt snout and aggressive temperament
Exceptional osmoregulatory ability allowing it to live and hunt in both full saltwater and freshwater rivers
Frequently travels thousands of kilometers up major rivers like the Amazon, Mississippi, and Zambezi
Possesses the highest bite force relative to body mass of any cartilaginous fish

facts_and_myths.claim: Bull sharks can survive indefinitely in freshwater lakes and rivers.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Their specialized kidneys and rectal glands recycle urea and regulate salt retention, allowing them to thrive in pure freshwater for years.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Bull sharks have been found over 3,000 kilometers up the Amazon River near Iquitos, Peru.

facts_and_myths.claim: Bull sharks are docile filter-feeders that only attack when stepped on in murky water.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Bull sharks are apex macropredators with extraordinarily high testosterone levels and an aggressive territorial hunting drive.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Bull sharks bump their prey with their blunt snouts before attacking to assess size and resistance.

name: Basking Shark
visual_anchor: A colossal basking shark cruising slowly near the surface with its cavernous mouth gaping wide to filter plankton.
core_traits: Second-largest living fish species on Earth, growing up to 10 to 12 meters in length
Enormous cavernous mouth equipped with bristly gill rakers to filter zooplankton and krill
Often seen slowly 'basking' along the surface with dorsal and caudal fins exposed
Completely harmless to humans despite intimidating, cavernous gaping jaws

facts_and_myths.claim: Basking sharks can filter over 2,000 tons of seawater every single hour.
facts_and_myths.explanation: By swimming forward with mouths agape at about 2 knots, their elongated gill slits filter huge volumes of water for planktonic crustaceans.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A basking shark's liver makes up nearly 25% of its entire body weight, filled with squalene oil that provides neutral buoyancy.

facts_and_myths.claim: Basking sharks hibernate buried deep in the mud of the ocean floor during winter.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Historical sailors believed they hibernated in sea mud, but satellite tagging proves they migrate thousands of miles into deep tropical waters during winter.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Basking sharks have hundreds of tiny teeth barely 5 millimeters long that play no role in feeding.

name: Whale Shark
visual_anchor: A gentle giant whale shark covered in luminous white polka dots gliding over a vibrant sunlit coral reef.
core_traits: Largest non-cetacean animal and undisputed largest living fish on the planet, exceeding 18 meters
Distinctive checkerboard pattern of pale yellow and white spots and stripes unique to each individual
Broad flattened head with a terminal mouth spanning up to 1.5 meters wide
Docile filter feeder sustaining its massive bulk on microscopic plankton, krill, and small fish

facts_and_myths.claim: Every whale shark has a unique spot pattern that functions like a human fingerprint.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Computer algorithms originally developed by NASA for mapping star constellations are used by researchers to identify individual whale sharks by spot patterns.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Whale shark skin can be up to 15 centimeters (6 inches) thick, making it one of the toughest hides in the animal kingdom.

facts_and_myths.claim: Whale sharks chew large squid and seals with hundreds of massive sharp teeth.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Whale sharks have about 3,000 tiny teeth in over 300 rows, but they do not use them to eat; they feed exclusively by suction-filtering plankton and fish eggs.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Whale sharks have tiny armored teeth (dermal denticles) surrounding their actual eyeballs to protect them.

name: Smalltooth Sawfish
visual_anchor: A prehistoric smalltooth sawfish swinging its tooth-studded rostrum back and forth over a sandy estuarine seabed.
core_traits: Critically endangered ray species characterized by a long, flat blade-like snout (rostrum) lined with teeth
The rostrum is packed with electro-receptors to detect hiding crabs and fish buried in sand
Swings its toothed saw side-to-side in slashing motions to impale and stun prey fish
Despite a shark-like silhouette, it is anatomically a ray with gill slits located underneath its body

facts_and_myths.claim: The teeth along a sawfish's rostrum are true replacement teeth like shark teeth.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The teeth on the rostrum are actually modified dermal denticles (scales); if broken or lost, they never grow back.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Female sawfish give birth to live young whose rostra are covered with a thick sheath of gelatinous cartilage to avoid injuring the mother.

facts_and_myths.claim: A sawfish can slice schooling fish in half with lightning-fast side-to-side swings of its saw.
facts_and_myths.explanation: High-speed underwater cameras demonstrate that sawfish slash their rostrum several times per second, stunning or severing prey before pinning them to the seabed.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Sawfish are capable of virgin birth (parthenogenesis) in the wild when mates are scarce.

name: Green Moray Eel
visual_anchor: A large green moray eel gaping its needle-filled jaws menacingly from a dark cavern in a tropical coral reef.
core_traits: One of the largest moray eels, reaching lengths up to 2.5 meters and weighing 30 kilograms
Appears brilliant green due to yellow mucus coating its dark blue-brown skin
Constantly opens and closes its mouth to pump oxygen-rich water over its gills
Equipped with a second set of internal pharyngeal jaws that pull food down its throat

facts_and_myths.claim: A moray eel's skin is naturally bright green beneath its surface.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Its skin is actually dark brown or slate gray; a thick layer of yellowish protective mucus covering the body creates the green optical appearance.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Moray eels possess 'Alien'-like pharyngeal jaws that shoot forward from the throat to latch onto prey and pull it backward into the esophagus.

facts_and_myths.claim: Moray eels open and close their mouths constantly as an aggressive threat display.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Opening and closing their jaws is simply how they breathe, forcing water through small gill holes behind the head.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Moray eels tie themselves into a knot to gain leverage when tearing large chunks of meat off prey.

name: Electric Eel
visual_anchor: A massive freshwater electric eel undulating slowly through murky Amazon river shallows, pulsing with bioelectric current.
core_traits: Famed bioelectric predator capable of generating electrical shocks up to 860 volts
Possesses three specialized electric organs composed of thousands of stacked electrocyte cells
Obligate air-breather that must surface every ten minutes to inhale atmospheric air
Biologically a knifefish (Gymnotiformes), completely unrelated to true marine eels

facts_and_myths.claim: The electric eel is biologically a true eel belonging to the order Anguilliformes.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Despite its common name and serpentine shape, it is a South American knifefish, more closely related to carp and catfish than true eels.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Over 80% of an electric eel's body length is occupied by electric organs, with its vital organs packed into the front 20%.

facts_and_myths.claim: An electric eel can leap upward out of the water to deliver a direct, amplified high-voltage shock.
facts_and_myths.explanation: When threatened by land predators like horses or caimans, it presses its chin against the attacker and discharges full voltage directly through the body.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Electric eels use low-voltage pulses like radar for navigation and communication in murky blackwater.

name: Red-Bellied Piranha
visual_anchor: A shoal of glittering silver-and-red piranhas with razor-sharp interlocking teeth schooling in the murky Amazon basin.
core_traits: Iconic Amazonian freshwater fish with a brilliant fiery orange-red throat and belly
Possesses a single row of razor-sharp, triangular interlocking teeth in each jaw
Incredible bite force relative to size, capable of snipping through bone and wire
Schools in defensive shoals to avoid predation by caimans, river dolphins, and otters

facts_and_myths.claim: A school of piranhas will regularly strip a live human adult to a clean skeleton in seconds.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Hollywood exaggeration; piranhas are shy, opportunistic omnivores and scavengers that feed mostly on fin clippings, insects, and dead fish.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Indigenous Amazonian peoples historically used dried piranha jaws and teeth as scissors and arrow-sharpening tools.

facts_and_myths.claim: Piranhas produce distinct barking and croaking sounds underwater when fighting or cornered.
facts_and_myths.explanation: By contracting rapid sonic muscles against their swim bladders, piranhas generate audible barking sounds to warn off competitors.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Piranha teeth interlock tightly like zippers, enabling them to shear off tissue rather than tear.

name: Great Barracuda
visual_anchor: A sleek, torpedo-shaped great barracuda with visible dagger teeth hanging motionless over a tropical coral reef.
core_traits: Fearsome open-water and reef ambush predator with an elongated torpedo-shaped body
Underhung lower jaw filled with two rows of dagger-like teeth of varying sizes
Capable of explosive ambush sprint bursts exceeding 45 km/h
Attracted to bright, shiny, reflective metallic objects in the water

facts_and_myths.claim: Barracudas are attracted to shiny metallic jewelry because it mimics the flash of fish scales.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Barracudas are visual hunters that strike at silver glints and bright flashes, mistaking wristwatches, rings, and knives for fluttering baitfish.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Consuming large tropical barracuda can cause ciguatera fish poisoning due to accumulated reef toxins.

facts_and_myths.claim: Barracudas actively track and hunt scuba divers as a favored food source.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Barracudas are curious and frequently shadow divers to watch for disturbed fish, but unprovoked attacks on humans are exceedingly rare.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A great barracuda can grow up to 2 meters long and weigh over 45 kilograms.

name: Swordfish
visual_anchor: A massive broadbill swordfish slashing through a school of mackerel with its long, flattened bill in the open Atlantic.
core_traits: Pelagic billfish renowned for its exceptionally long, flattened, sword-like bill
Bill is flat and broad like a sword rather than round like a marlin's spear
Adults lose all teeth and scales as they mature, becoming completely smooth-skinned
Possesses specialized heating tissue near the eyes to enhance vision in freezing deep water

facts_and_myths.claim: Swordfish use their long bill to spear prey like a shish kebab before eating.
facts_and_myths.explanation: They slash their bill from side to side to stun, maim, or cut prey fish in schools, then circle back to swallow the disabled pieces.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Swordfish have a specialized brain and eye heater organ that keeps retinal temperatures 10 to 15 degrees above ocean depths.

facts_and_myths.claim: Adult swordfish are completely scale-less and toothless.
facts_and_myths.explanation: While juveniles have scales and fine teeth, both are entirely shed by the time the fish reaches about one meter in length.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Swordfish bills have been found lodged deep inside the wooden hulls of ancient sailing ships and submarines.

name: Blue Marlin
visual_anchor: A colossal cobalt-blue marlin erupting out of ocean swell with glistening sides and an outstretched spear bill.
core_traits: Among the largest and most powerful apex bony fish in the world, females exceeding 600 kilograms
Cobalt-blue upper body and silvery-white belly, capable of rapidly flashing electric blue stripes
Long, cylindrical, spear-like upper bill used to stun pelagic prey like tuna and squid
Legendary sport fish celebrated in Ernest Hemingway's novel The Old Man and the Sea

facts_and_myths.claim: Blue marlins can instantly change color and flash glowing stripes when hunting.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Specialized chromatophores and light-reflecting cells allow a marlin to flash electric blue and violet bands, which confuses schooling prey and signals other marlins.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Female blue marlins grow up to four times heavier than males, with only females reaching 'grander' status (over 1,000 lbs).

facts_and_myths.claim: Blue marlins have a broad, flat sword bill identical to that of a broadbill swordfish.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A marlin's bill is round and cylindrical in cross-section like a spear, whereas a swordfish bill is flat and oval like a broadsword.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Blue marlins can swim at speeds of up to 80 km/h in deep open oceans.

name: Sailfish
visual_anchor: A spectacular sailfish cutting through the water with its towering cobalt sail fin fully raised above the surface.
core_traits: Widely celebrated as one of the fastest marine animals on Earth, clocking speeds over 100 km/h
Enormous sail-like dorsal fin that stretches almost the entire length of its back
Folds the massive sail flat into a dorsal groove during high-speed swimming to reduce drag
Raises the sail to herd, corral, and intimidate schools of sardine prey

facts_and_myths.claim: Sailfish always swim with their enormous sail fin raised upright.
facts_and_myths.explanation: They keep their sail folded neatly into a sleek groove on their back when cruising or sprinting, raising it only when braking, turning, or herding fish.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Sailfish work cooperatively in packs, taking turns raising sails to create a wall that traps schooling sardines.

facts_and_myths.claim: Sailfish can tap individual sardines with the tip of their bill without alerting the rest of the school.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Their bill is so slender that it can slip into a school with minimal hydrodynamic wake, allowing the sailfish to gently knock prey off-balance before swallowing it.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Sailfish grow from tiny 3-millimeter larvae to over 1.5 meters long in their very first year of life.

name: Pufferfish
visual_anchor: A globular inflated pufferfish hovering defensively near coral with skin bristling with small sharp spines.
core_traits: Globular marine fish famous for inflating its elastic stomach with water to become an unswallowable sphere
Contains tetrodotoxin, an extraordinarily potent neurotoxin up to 1,200 times deadlier than cyanide
Four fused front teeth forming a parrot-like beak capable of crushing clams and crabs
Considered a high-risk gourmet delicacy in Japan called 'fugu', prepared only by licensed chefs

facts_and_myths.claim: Pufferfish inflate their bodies primarily by gulping large volumes of air.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Under natural conditions underwater, they rapidly pump water into their specialized highly elastic stomach; they swallow air only if pulled out of the sea.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A single pufferfish contains enough tetrodotoxin in its liver and ovaries to kill 30 adult humans.

facts_and_myths.claim: Male white-spotted pufferfish create intricate symmetrical geometric sand circles on the seabed to attract mates.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Small 12-centimeter males spend over a week tirelessly carving 2-meter wide 'underwater crop circles' in sandy ocean beds using their fins.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Dolphins have been observed gently chewing and passing pufferfish around, seemingly entering a trance-like state from low toxin doses.

name: Deep Sea Anglerfish
visual_anchor: A ghoulish female anglerfish suspended in inky black abyss, illuminated only by a glowing bioluminescent lure dangling over needle teeth.
core_traits: Bizarre deep-sea predator inhabiting the bathypelagic abyss in perpetual darkness
Bears a modified dorsal spine called an ilicium tipped with a bioluminescent glowing lure (esca)
Enormous expandable jaws lined with long, translucent needle-like teeth angled inward
Extreme sexual parasitism where tiny dwarf males fuse permanently onto the female's body

facts_and_myths.claim: The glowing light on an anglerfish's lure is produced directly by the fish's own glowing cells.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The light is created by a symbiotic colony of bioluminescent bacteria (Photobacterium) living inside the fleshy lure tip.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Dwarf male anglerfish bite into the female, dissolve their own mouths and internal organs, and become permanent sperm-producing appendages.

facts_and_myths.claim: Deep-sea anglerfish can swallow prey twice as large as their own body size.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Their stomach and ribcage are exceptionally elastic, allowing them to engulf and digest large meals in food-scarce abyssal depths.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Only female anglerfish possess the famous fishing rod and glowing lure; males lack them entirely.

name: Red Lionfish
visual_anchor: A flamboyant red lionfish hovering over coral with flowing fan-like pectoral fins and venomous striped spines radiating outward.
core_traits: Visually stunning reef fish featuring dramatic maroon, brown, and white zebra stripes
Equipped with 18 venomous needle-sharp dorsal, pelvic, and anal spine rays
Uses wide, fan-like pectoral fins like wings to herd and corner small fish against coral crevices
Highly invasive predator in the Caribbean and Atlantic, severely disrupting native reef ecosystems

facts_and_myths.claim: A lionfish can sting predators by actively spitting venom through its mouth.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Lionfish venom is purely defensive and delivered mechanically through grooved spines on their fins when stepped on or bitten.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A single lionfish can reduce the recruitment of juvenile native reef fish on a coral head by nearly 80% in five weeks.

facts_and_myths.claim: Lionfish stomachs can expand up to thirty times their normal empty volume.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Their stomachs are enormously elastic, allowing them to binge on prey fish until they become obese in waters with no natural predators.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Despite deadly venomous spines, lionfish flesh is non-toxic, delicious, and widely served as sustainable seafood.

name: Southern Stingray
visual_anchor: A diamond-shaped southern stingray gliding gracefully along a sun-dappled sandy seabed in shallow turquoise water.
core_traits: Flat diamond-shaped cartilaginous fish adapted for life on sandy shallow sea floors
Long whip-like tail equipped with one or more serrated venomous barbs near the base
Spiracles located on top of the head behind the eyes allow breathing while buried in sand
Mouth with flat crushing dental plates on the underside to grind clams and crabs

facts_and_myths.claim: Stingrays use their venomous tail barbs to attack and stun swimming fish while hunting.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The tail barb is strictly a defensive weapon used when stepped on or grabbed by sharks; they hunt bottom invertebrates using suction and crushing jaws.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The 'stingray shuffle' - sliding feet along sandy shallows - warns buried stingrays to swim away, preventing painful stings.

facts_and_myths.claim: Stingrays locate buried prey on the ocean floor using electrical sensors called ampullae of Lorenzini.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because their eyes are on top of their head and mouth is underneath, they rely entirely on electroreception and smell to find food in the sand.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A stingray's tail barb is serrated like a hunting knife and continuously replaced throughout life.

name: Moon Jellyfish
visual_anchor: A translucent moon jellyfish drifting gently in clear blue water with four distinct purple horseshoe-shaped gonads glowing in its bell.
core_traits: Translucent, saucer-shaped pelagic cnidarian recognizable by four purple or pink horseshoe gonads
Consists of approximately 95% water and completely lacks a brain, heart, bones, or blood
Fringed with hundreds of delicate marginal tentacles that trap microscopic plankton in mucus
Possesses extremely mild stinging cells that are virtually harmless to human skin

facts_and_myths.claim: A moon jellyfish possesses a central nervous system and a beating heart to pump fluids.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Moon jellies lack all centralized organs; they have a simple nerve net that coordinates swimming pulses and senses gravity and light.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Moon jellyfish were sent into space aboard the Space Shuttle Columbia in 1991 to study how microgravity affects development.

facts_and_myths.claim: Moon jellyfish can revert their life cycle and clone themselves through polyp budding.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Their complex life cycle includes benthic polyps that undergo strobilation, budding off dozens of genetically identical baby ephyrae.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The four distinct horseshoe shapes visible through the transparent bell are the jellyfish's reproductive organs.

name: Box Jellyfish
visual_anchor: A spectral pale-blue box jellyfish trailing three-meter venomous tentacles through calm coastal waters off northern Australia.
core_traits: Cube-shaped medusa widely considered the most venomous marine creature on the planet
Tentacles carry millions of nematocysts delivering lethal venom that can stop a human heart in minutes
Possesses 24 sophisticated eyes arranged in clusters, including eyes with true lenses and retinas
Active hunter capable of directed swimming at speeds up to 6 km/h rather than just drifting

facts_and_myths.claim: Box jellyfish drift entirely at the mercy of ocean currents with no ability to steer.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Unlike true jellyfish, box jellyfish (cubozoans) are vigorous active swimmers that steer using a velarium shelf and navigate around obstacles.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Box jellyfish have true image-forming eyes complete with lenses and corneas, allowing them to actively avoid dark shadows.

facts_and_myths.claim: The venom of a box jellyfish can cause fatal cardiovascular arrest in under five minutes.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Its potent cardiotoxins attack heart muscle cells, causing excruciating pain, paralysis, and rapid cardiac arrest before victims can reach shore.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Green sea turtles are completely immune to box jellyfish venom and consume them like gelatin snacks.

name: Sea Anemone
visual_anchor: A colorful cluster of sea anemones with waving fluorescent tentacles attached firmly to a coral reef rock face.
core_traits: Sedentary marine predatory polyp named after the terrestrial anemone flower
Columnar body anchored to hard substrate by an adhesive pedal disc
Ring of stinging tentacles armed with nematocysts surrounding a central mouth
